scenes.tts: A mushroom pops up on a dead log. It does not walk, swim or fly away. For a long time, many scientists grouped mushrooms with plants. Today mushrooms have their own kingdom. DNA shows they are closer to you than to an oak tree. How did that happen?

scenes.narration: A mushroom pops up on a dead log. It does not walk, swim or fly away. For a long time, many scientists grouped mushrooms with plants. Today mushrooms have their own kingdom. DNA shows they are closer to you than to an oak tree. How did that happen?

scenes.tts: Scientists sort living things with four clues. Does the cell have a nucleus? A nucleus is the part of a cell that holds its DNA. Which cell parts are there? A cell wall is a stiff layer outside the cell. A chloroplast is a green part where a cell makes sugar using light. Is it one cell or many? Does it make its own food or take food in?
scenes.visual: Four clue cards appear one by one: nucleus, cell parts (wall, chloroplast), one or many cells, food.
scenes.narration: Scientists sort living things with four clues. Does the cell have a nucleus? A nucleus is the part of a cell that holds its DNA. Which cell parts are there? A cell wall is a stiff layer outside the cell. A chloroplast is a green part where a cell makes sugar using light. Is it one cell or many? Does it make its own food or take food in?

scenes.tts: The first clue splits life into cells with a nucleus and cells without one. Genes and chemistry split the cells without a nucleus into two domains. So life has three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. Eukarya holds all organisms whose cells have a nucleus. Many textbooks use six kingdoms, and four are inside Eukarya.
scenes.visual: Cells with and without a nucleus; three domain boxes; Eukarya holds four kingdoms.

scenes.tts: A mushroom's cells have a nucleus and a cell wall. They have no chloroplasts, so a fungus cannot make sugar from light. It takes in food from what it grows on. These clues put fungi in their own kingdom, not with plants.
scenes.visual: The mushroom cell is checked against the clues; plant card loses the chloroplast match; fungi box.
scenes.narration: A mushroom's cells have a nucleus and a cell wall. They have no chloroplasts, so a fungus cannot make sugar from light. It takes in food from what it grows on. These clues put fungi in their own kingdom, not with plants.

scenes.tts: Then came DNA. A DNA sequence is the order of the chemical letters in a stretch of DNA. The more alike two organisms' DNA sequences are, the more closely related they are. A common ancestor is an organism that two groups both descend from. Comparing DNA and proteins put fungi closer to animals than to plants.
scenes.visual: Two rows of blocks with matches highlighted; a taller or shorter match bar; common ancestor.
scenes.narration: Then came DNA. A DNA sequence is the order of the chemical letters in a stretch of DNA. The more alike two organisms' DNA sequences are, the more closely related they are. A common ancestor is an organism that two groups both descend from. Comparing DNA and proteins put fungi closer to animals than to plants.

scenes.tts: That does not make a mushroom an animal. It means fungi and animals share a more recent common ancestor than either shares with plants. New tools give new evidence, from microscopes to DNA comparisons. New evidence can change how living things are grouped. So DNA can move a living thing to a new group.
